prompt.context: Your client is WorkIt, an insurance firm that sells workers' compensation insurance policies exclusively. Workers' compensation is an insurance policy that companies purchase to protect themselves from lengthy litigation and unexpected and incredibly high legal fees related to employees who are injured at work. Workers' compensation is paid by the company on a per-employee basis each month and in exchange, the policy covers medical, indemnity, and other expenses. For example, if an employee falls off a ladder and breaks a leg, workers' compensation pays for the employee's medical bills and indemnity or lost wages. The policy also covers other related expenses. Companies are required by state law to purchase workers' compensation plans. WorkIt has been successful in North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia but is considering entering a new state.
prompt.question: WorkIt would like your help to determine if this is a good idea. Should WorkIt expand into a new state, and if so, where?

clarifying_info.a: The first prompt is open-ended; goals will emerge as the case proceeds. Profit is a big concern, but qualitative issues also matter.

clarifying_info.q: Does WorkIt sell any other insurance products?
clarifying_info.a: No, WorkIt sells workers' compensation insurance exclusively.

clarifying_info.q: What components does a workers' compensation policy cover?
clarifying_info.a: It covers three categories: Medical (e.g., hospital bills), Indemnity (e.g., lost wages), and Expenses (e.g., overhead, benefit delivery, occasional attorney fees).

exhibits.title: Total Employment (Ths.)
exhibits.shows: A table listing 9 southern states with total employment (thousands) and percentage of employees injured each year, from which total injured can be derived.

exhibits.title: Growth in Cost Per Claim
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing percent change in cost per claim for each state, comparing 2012-to-2013 and 2013-to-2014 periods. Values range from approximately -10% to +10%.
exhibits.data: States shown: AR, WV, MS, TN, FL, TX, LA, VA, AL. AL shows large negative change 2013-2014. MS and TN show variability. VA shows relatively stable, near-zero change across both periods.

exhibits.title: Medical Costs Per Claim (2013)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing average medical cost per claim by state in 2013, ranging from roughly $5,000 to $18,000.
exhibits.data: Approximate values from chart: AL ~$17,500; VA ~$16,000; TN ~$11,000; MS ~$10,000; AR ~$5,000; WV ~$5,000 (exact values confirmed in Prompt 3 solution)

exhibits.title: Breakdown of Total Costs
exhibits.shows: A pie chart showing the proportional breakdown of all workers' compensation costs into three categories.

framework: Revenue & Profitability: premium revenue (101% of total costs), cost structure (medical, indemnity, expenses), profit margin (1% of total costs)
Market Size & Fit: number of injured employees per state, WorkIt's size criteria (30,000–70,000 cases), ability to control entire state market
Competitive Landscape: existing players in each state, risk of bidding wars, market share achievability
Regulatory & Legal Environment: state-specific policy changes, hospital reform, judicial reform, impact on cost trends
Operational Capabilities: cost of market entry, ability to manage operations remotely, need for local legal or operational teams
Geographic & Network Fit: proximity to existing SE footprint (NC, SC, GA), regional expansion logic

questions.prompt: Which of the 9 candidate states meet WorkIt's size criteria (between 30,000 and 70,000 injured employees per year)?
questions.guidance: Candidate multiplies total employment by injury rate for each state and filters to those with 30,000–70,000 injuries. FL (154k), LA (80k), TX (456k) are too large; AR (24k) and WV (16k) are too small. Qualifying states: AL (40k), MS (46k), TN (56k), VA (39k).

math.setup: Total injured (ths.) = Total employed (ths.) x % injured. Filter: 30 <= total injured <= 70.
math.answer: Four qualifying states: AL, MS, TN, VA

questions.prompt: Calculate WorkIt's annual profit in each of the four qualifying states (AL, MS, TN, VA). WorkIt's revenue is a flat 101% of total costs.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates recognize that profit = 1% of total costs, shortcutting the full revenue calculation. They use Exhibit 3 for medical cost per claim and Exhibit 4 to gross up (medical is 50% of total costs, so total cost = medical cost x 2). Note: figures are in thousands, so $14,000 profit in AL represents $14,000,000.

math.setup: Step 1: Total medical cost = injuries (ths.) x medical cost per claim. Step 2: Total cost = total medical x 2 (since medical = 50% of total). Step 3: Profit = total cost x 1%.
steps: MS: 46 x $10,000 = $460,000k medical; x2 = $920,000k total cost; profit = $9,200k ($9.2M)
math.answer: AL: $14M; TN: $12.3M; VA: $12.5M; MS: $9.2M. Alabama has the highest absolute profit potential.

questions.prompt: WorkIt is concerned about recent policy changes and hospital and judicial reform that could impact its 1% commission. Without doing any math, which state should WorkIt now consider most attractive?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit 2 (Growth in Cost Per Claim) to assess cost trend stability. AL is now less attractive because total costs have decreased significantly in both periods — if costs fall, so does the 1% profit. MS and TN show variability and recent cost decreases, making future profits unpredictable. VA shows the most stable cost trend (near-zero change), making it the most predictable and therefore most attractive state.

brainstorming.prompt: What else should WorkIt research before making a final expansion decision?

categories.name: Additional Costs
ideas: Future changes to fixed costs (staffing, infrastructure)
Future changes to variable costs (claims frequency, severity trends)
Cost of market entry and establishing operations in a new state

categories.name: Competition
ideas: Which competitors are currently operating in each qualifying state?
Risk of a bidding war to win the state contract

categories.name: Regulatory & Legal
ideas: State-specific legal and judicial reforms beyond what is in the data
Whether WorkIt needs to hire a dedicated local legal team
Any state-specific restrictions or licensing requirements that could complicate entry

categories.name: Company Capabilities
ideas: Can WorkIt operate successfully from its current SE base?
Does WorkIt have the operational infrastructure to scale to a new state?
Would a remote operating model reduce effectiveness or increase cost?

recommendation: WorkIt should expand, and Virginia is the recommended state.
Virginia has the second-highest profit potential ($12.5M, close to AL's $14M) while showing the most stable cost trends — making it the most predictable and defensible long-term market.
risks: Cost compression: if hospital/judicial reforms reduce costs further, WorkIt's 1% margin shrinks proportionally
Competitive risk: an entrenched incumbent could trigger a bidding war that erodes profitability
Regulatory risk: Virginia-specific policy changes not yet captured in available data
Operational risk: managing a geographically adjacent but new state market stretches existing capabilities
next_steps: Identify current workers' compensation providers in Virginia and assess competitive dynamics
Quantify cost of market entry (licensing, staffing, legal, IT)
Conduct a deeper regulatory review of Virginia policy trends
Evaluate whether WorkIt's existing NC/SC/GA infrastructure can support a Virginia expansion with minimal incremental overhead
Assess whether WorkIt should also evaluate diversifying beyond workers' compensation to reduce commission-compression risk
